title: Act III, Scene I
focus: 'To be, or not to be' and the nunnery scene

teacherSummary.text: Rosencrantz and Guildenstern report failure. Claudius and Polonius hide to watch Hamlet with Ophelia. Hamlet meditates on life, death and action. Ophelia returns his gifts; he denies loving her, tells her to go to a nunnery, and rails against marriage. Claudius decides to send Hamlet to England.

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: Excerpt-based (Middle School support track; this play is above the grades 6–8 complexity band, so work from the passage your teacher selects). In “Act III, Scene I,” how does Shakespeare show 'To be, or not to be' and the nunnery scene? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the passage, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the structure you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In Act III, Scene I, how does Shakespeare develop the idea of 'To be, or not to be' and the nunnery scene? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the structure in the scene helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Act III, Scene I develops the idea of 'To be, or not to be' and the nunnery scene. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of structure and characterization shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of Act III, Scene I (where it begins, turns and ends) and its structure shape the reader's understanding of 'To be, or not to be' and the nunnery scene. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what Act III, Scene I suggests about 'To be, or not to be' and the nunnery scene. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the scene's structure and characterization), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how William Shakespeare uses structure in Act III, Scene I to complicate the reader's understanding of 'To be, or not to be' and the nunnery scene. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Act III, Scene I within its historical and literary context and argue how the scene's treatment of 'To be, or not to be' and the nunnery scene responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Act III, Scene I alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the scene's handling of 'To be, or not to be' and the nunnery scene follows or bends those conventions, using the structure as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Act III, Scene I and its treatment of 'To be, or not to be' and the nunnery scene. State your method, show what it reveals in the scene's structure and characterization, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Act III, Scene I as evidence for a larger claim about 'To be, or not to be' and the nunnery scene in Hamlet. Connect close reading of the scene to the whole play, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Act III, Scene I as a hinge in the play's larger treatment of 'To be, or not to be' and the nunnery scene. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Hamlet.

symbolsAndMotifs.name: poison and ears
symbolsAndMotifs.explanation: Old Hamlet was poisoned through the ear; lies poured into ears, and poison returns at the end. In this scene: “him; / And I’ll be placed, so please you, in the ear / Of all their conference. If she find him not, / To England” (Act III, Scene I, Polonius (speech 44)).

symbolsAndMotifs.name: acting and seeming
symbolsAndMotifs.explanation: "Seems, madam! nay it is": performance, the players, feigned madness and the Mousetrap. In this scene: “Madam, it so fell out, that certain players / We o’er-raught on the way: of these we told him; / And” (Act III, Scene I, Rosencrantz (speech 9)).

routine: Bell-ringer: post one literal and one evaluative question; students jot before talking (wait time).
Discussion (10 min): run the focus questions for the class level in order, literal to evaluative; think-pair-share every DOK 3/4 item.
After each answer, use a follow-up probe before moving on; ask a second student to agree, extend or challenge.
Exit: each student writes one question of their own (student-generated) for tomorrow’s opener.

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the scene to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.

contentNotes.teacherNote: 'To be, or not to be' weighs living against dying. Use the safe-messaging script; keep the discussion on Hamlet's reasoning about action and uncertainty, and name where to find support.
contentNotes.studentPreview: This speech considers whether life is worth living. Support is available if this is hard to read.
contentNotes.suggestedLanguage: “What stops Hamlet from acting, according to the speech?”

safeMessaging.teacherScript: Discuss the character's despair and what the text does with it; do not dwell on methods. Before the lesson, remind students that support is available and how to reach the counselor. Check in privately with any student who seems affected and follow your school's referral protocol.
safeMessaging.studentResource: If you or someone you know is struggling or thinking about suicide, call or text 988 (Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, U.S.) or talk with a school counselor today.
safeMessaging.counselorPrompt: Let a counselor know in advance that this scene is being taught.
